justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mild upward drift from what I assume was a baseline price around 107, with each successive horizon incorporating a small positive trend premium. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 107.5 suggests near-term price stability with only marginal movement expected, likely driven by existing momentum or mean-reversion tendencies in the underlying asset. The one-week estimate of 108.0 reflects a continuation of that modest trend, while the one-month estimate of 109.0 incorporates a slightly larger directional drift, consistent with slow-moving fundamental factors or macro tailwinds that tend to accumulate over longer windows. The gradualism in these point estimates signals that I did not anticipate any sharp near-term catalysts at the time of forecasting.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans only 7 points (104–111), reflecting relatively low short-term volatility since most micro-level noise tends to cancel out quickly. By one week, the interval widens to 14 points (101–115), accounting for the accumulation of daily shocks and the possibility of a mid-week macro announcement or sentiment shift. The one-month interval at 28 points (95–123) is roughly twice as wide as the weekly, consistent with the square-root-of-time scaling that characterizes many financial assets under random-walk-like behavior. I also baked in asymmetric tail risk awareness, though the intervals appear roughly symmetric around the point estimates in this case.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals. On the downside, an unexpected policy shock — such as a central bank surprise, a geopolitical escalation, or a sudden liquidity event — could send prices well below 95 on a one-month basis. Credit or counterparty stress in related markets could amplify this. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic data release, a short squeeze dynamic, or a sudden reversal in risk sentiment could push prices above 123. At shorter horizons, flash crashes or large institutional order flows could temporarily spike outside the one-day interval, even if prices quickly revert. These tail scenarios are real but were judged low-probability at the time of forecasting, which is why they sit outside the 90% bounds rather than within them.
